Yeah... We've all heard this. It's funny; it seems to make sense. But lately... I've been wondering.

The Mahabharata (165.34-35 -- or less than 5 lines away) mentions all the disgusting shit-races born from a horse's cow's (edit) ass. No, seriously. There are Palavis(Persians), Yavanas (Ionians/Greeks), Barbaras (???), Sakas (Skythians), a bunch of others, then Mlecchas (foreigners). My question is why are "barbaras" (barbarians) listed separately among individual races, if there is a catch-all Mlecchas at the end of the list? So, I looked in other literature -- Barbaras are berbers... Alrighty, then... but barbara is also a "stutterer". Weird. Even weirder that Greeks and Indians would be using the same term, with the same etymology. Homer sang about Barbarians. The earliest I've found in India is about 500 AD.

It seems more likely that Greeks and Indians met a common neighbor than either a) they developed the same onomatopoeia for foreign speech, or b) had a common Indo-European substrate for "foreigner". But then, who are these Barbars? Were they Berbers? I can't even tell why Berbers are called "Berbers". In their own language, they are Amazigh. But Arabs also call them "Berbers". Here, it seems more likely that everyone had called them Barbarians...
Mlecchas seems like It's describing Civil foreigners, while in greek barbaros is literally the antonym to politēs meaning citizen, polite, or civil.

Or maybe barbarian and mlecchas are just onomatopoeic words describing how people sound talking in their native languages. Barbarian for the languages with hard stops and lots of front mouth action, mlecchas for slurring back mouth languages.

It's possible, but mleccha looks like it derives from a non-IE root (I'm guessing Tamil). I like this idea of "ching-chongs" and "durka-durkas". I can see that happening now.

Edit to add: !!! There is an unknown kingdom familiar to Sumer called "Meluhha". Intradasting.
Stereotypes aren't new, not even close. And with intercontinental trade happening having a foreign word pop up in a language isn't terribly uncommon, especially if it's super funny.
